title: Image Forensics and Geolocation OSINT: Metadata, Reverse Search, Shadows and Verification
intro: Image and geolocation OSINT is the practice of extracting evidence from a picture's embedded metadata and its visible content to establish where it came from, where it was taken, and when. The goal of this lesson is to let you verify lures, leaked screenshots, and actor-posted media with calibrated confidence, and to audit what your own organization's images reveal.

sections.heading: Why a SOC analyzes images
sections.content:
Images arrive in a SOC far more often than people expect, and each arrival is a claim that needs testing. Four recurring situations justify a repeatable method.

**Phishing and fraud lures.** A fake-recruiter or romance-style approach against an employee usually carries a profile photo. If that photo is a stolen image, the persona is synthetic, and the same image will often appear under several names. Reverse image search turns a vague suspicion into a documented reuse chain. Lures also embed logos, fake invoices, and screenshots of 'shared documents' whose visual details (fonts, layout, UI chrome) reveal they were assembled by hand.

**Fake or inflated leak claims.** Extortion groups and hacktivists post screenshots as 'proof of breach'. Many are recycled from older incidents, taken from a vendor demo, or edited. Your job is not to decide whether the breach happened (only your own telemetry can do that) but to decide how much weight the image deserves in the incident narrative and in the message sent to leadership.

**Threat-actor media.** Actors post photos of themselves, their desks, their travel, or their victims' premises. Backgrounds, window views, and signage can narrow a location, and timestamps embedded in files can contradict a claimed timeline. This is also where ethics and law start to matter, covered later in this lesson.

**Your own exposure.** Marketing photos, conference pictures, job-ad office tours, and employee social posts can leak GPS coordinates, device serial numbers, badge designs, whiteboard contents, and visible screens. Attackers do the same analysis against you during reconnaissance, so defenders should run it first.

**The two questions to ask every time.** First, what does the file itself say (metadata, structure, compression history)? Second, what does the picture show (content that can be placed in space and time)? These two evidence streams are independent. Agreement between them raises confidence; disagreement is the most valuable finding.

**What you must keep in mind.** Every technique in this lesson produces leads and probabilities, not proof. A stripped file proves nothing, a clean error-level scan proves nothing, and a reverse search with no hits proves nothing. Analysts who state findings as 'consistent with', 'inconsistent with', and 'not determinable' are right far more often than analysts who state them as verdicts.

sections.heading: Image metadata: EXIF, IPTC and XMP
sections.content:
**What it is.** Metadata is data about the image stored inside the file, like the luggage tag on a suitcase: it describes the contents without being the contents. Three families matter. EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) is written by the camera or phone and is built on the TIFF tag structure. IPTC fields are editorial: caption, creator, copyright, keywords, usually added by photo software or news desks. XMP is an XML packet that editing software uses to record creator tool, edit history, and rights information.

**How it is stored.** In a JPEG, EXIF lives in an APP1 segment near the start of the file as a table of tags, with sub-tables for GPS data and for camera maker-specific notes. PNG files normally carry no camera EXIF, though an eXIf chunk and text chunks are possible. That is why a true screenshot rarely has a camera model but often has dimensions matching a known device or display resolution.

**Reading it with ExifTool.** ExifTool is the standard tool and reads nearly every format. Useful invocations:

- exiftool -a -G1 -s file.jpg shows all tags including duplicates, with the group name that tells you which block each came from.
- exiftool -n -gps:all file.jpg shows GPS in raw decimal numbers, avoiding degree-minute formatting errors.
- exiftool -csv -r ./folder > audit.csv dumps a whole directory recursively for bulk review.
- exiftool -ee -G3 -api largefilesupport=1 video.mp4 extracts per-sample data embedded in video.

| Field | What it tells you | Typical pitfall |
|---|---|---|
| Make, Model | Capture device | Easily edited; absent after most platform uploads |
| DateTimeOriginal | Local time of shutter press | Has no time zone unless OffsetTimeOriginal exists |
| CreateDate, ModifyDate | File creation and last edit | ModifyDate later than DateTimeOriginal suggests editing, not proof |
| GPSLatitude, GPSLongitude | Where the device thought it was | Can be absent, spoofed, or from a stale fix |
| GPSDateStamp, GPSTimeStamp | UTC time from satellites | Compare with DateTimeOriginal for clock tampering |
| GPSImgDirection | Compass heading of the lens | Useful to confirm view direction |
| Software, CreatorTool | Editor or firmware | Presence of an editor means a re-save happened |
| SerialNumber, LensModel | Device-level identifiers | Links multiple images to one camera |
| ThumbnailImage | Embedded preview | May show the pre-edit picture |

**What matters for the analyst.** Check internal consistency first: a Model that does not support the stated lens, a thumbnail that differs from the main image, or GPS time that disagrees with local time by an impossible offset are stronger signals than any single value.

sections.heading: Why platforms strip metadata and what that means for you
sections.content:
**Stripping is the norm, not a signal.** Most large social and messaging services re-encode uploads and remove EXIF, partly to save bytes and partly to protect users from accidentally publishing their home coordinates. Some keep orientation or color-profile tags and discard the rest; some keep certain fields for the account holder but not for viewers. Behavior also differs between the web upload path, the mobile app, and the 'send as file' option in messengers. So an image you pull from a social post with no EXIF tells you almost nothing, while the same image obtained as an original attachment, a direct download from a paste site, or a file from a phishing email may be rich in metadata.

**Where original files appear.** Email attachments, cloud-storage share links, forum uploads, and extortion sites often serve the file unmodified. Always ask 'what is the closest copy to the source I can obtain?' and preserve the received file with a hash before opening or converting it. Re-saving, screenshotting, or opening and exporting from an editor destroys evidence.

**The privacy lesson.** Phones record GPS in photos by default unless the camera permission is withheld. A picture of a new product prototype taken at a home office, uploaded to a site that does not strip metadata, can reveal a home address. Real incidents of this kind are well documented: location leaks from images have exposed private residences and sensitive facilities.

**Auditing your own organization.** Run a periodic exposure check:

1. Inventory public image sources: website media library, press kit, job-ad photos, event galleries, official social accounts, public repositories and documentation sites.
2. Download originals the same way an outsider would, and run exiftool recursively with a filter such as -if '$GPSLatitude' -filename to list only files that carry coordinates.
3. Also list Artist, Copyright, SerialNumber, Software, and any internal path or username inside XMP history.
4. Remediate at the publishing pipeline, not file by file: strip with exiftool -all= or the CMS image processor, then re-test.
5. Remember that content leaks too: badge photos, monitors, whiteboards, network diagrams, and window views are not metadata and survive stripping.

**Questions to ask.** Which copy is this? Has it been re-encoded? Which tags would a device have written and which are missing? Who benefits if the tags were removed or added?

sections.heading: Reverse image search: finding origin and reuse
sections.content:
**What it does.** Reverse image search compares an image against an index of previously crawled pictures and returns exact or similar matches. Think of it as asking a very large library 'where have I seen this before?' Its most common SOC uses are finding the first appearance of an image, proving a profile photo was lifted from another person, spotting a leak screenshot reused from an older incident, and identifying a stock or vendor-demo image used as 'proof'.

**Engines differ, so use several.** No single index covers the web. Each engine has different crawl coverage and matching algorithms.

| Engine | Strengths | Weaknesses | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google Lens / Google Images | Very large index, object and text recognition, good on products and mainstream pages | Tends to return visually similar rather than exact matches; weaker on obscure forums | General first pass, products, text inside images |
| Yandex Images | Strong similarity matching, good with landmarks and with pages from Eastern Europe and Russian-language social sites | Results change over time; regional bias | Locating scenes, finding persona reuse on regional sites |
| TinEye | Exact and modified-copy matching, can sort by oldest crawl date or by size | Smaller index, little semantic understanding | Establishing the earliest known appearance |
| Bing Visual Search | Decent object cropping and shopping matches | Smaller coverage of social sites | Cross-checking and cropped regions |

**Technique.** Crop to the interesting region, because background clutter lowers match quality. Try flipped versions, since mirrored reposts are common. Search several sub-regions: the face region of a persona photo, a distinctive building, a logo. Search the highest-resolution copy you have. When you find a match, record the URL, crawl date, and a hash or screenshot, since pages disappear.

**Pitfalls.** Reverse search is not exhaustive: no hits does not mean the image is original, only that it is absent from the indexed set. Private messaging apps, closed groups, and paywalled content are not indexed. A first match date is the first date the engine saw it, not the date it was created. Beware of AI-generated personas: a clean result for a face may mean it was newly generated, not that it is genuine.

**Face search services.** Services that match faces across the web raise biometric-privacy and data-protection issues, and may be unlawful for an employer to use on individuals in some jurisdictions. Consult legal counsel and prefer image-level matching for investigating a lure.

sections.heading: Geolocation from image content
sections.content:
**What it is.** Geolocation is placing a photo on the map using only what is visible, when metadata is missing or untrusted. It works like a detective narrowing a suspect list: each clue removes possibilities until a small area remains. The discipline is to work from coarse to fine, and to hold more than one hypothesis until evidence eliminates it.

**Step 1: country and region.** Look for text and language on signs, writing systems, and the way phone numbers and addresses are formatted. Driving side (traffic direction, position of the driver) eliminates large parts of the world. Road markings carry strong regional signal: center line color (yellow versus white), edge lines, dashed patterns, and bollard shapes. License-plate shape, color, and character layout differ by country and often by region; plates also show a flag, an emblem strip, or a regional code. Utility poles, power-line designs, and electrical sockets in indoor photos add more.

**Step 2: environment.** Vegetation, soil color, terrain, and climate cues (snow, dust, palm trees, rice paddies) narrow the latitude band. Architecture helps: roof styles, building materials, window shutters, balcony designs, and street furniture often cluster regionally. Sun direction in the northern versus southern hemisphere and overall light quality also give a rough sense of latitude.

**Step 3: anchor features.** Find something unique: a church with a distinctive tower, a bridge, a skyline profile, a mountain ridge line, a rail crossing, or a unique shop sign. Search distinctive business names in map services. Then confirm with satellite imagery and street-level imagery, matching road geometry, building shapes, and the relative position of features. Use the viewing direction: if you believe the camera stood at point A looking at B, the skyline and roads must line up from that vantage.

**Step 4: validate.** A location is established only when several independent features match and no major element contradicts. Check the date of the satellite or street-level imagery, since the scene may have changed.

**Pitfalls.** Staged scenes, stock backgrounds, and cropped photos all mislead. Street-level imagery is often years old. A bilingual sign proves little in regions with several languages. Confirmation bias is the main error: analysts who want a particular answer find supporting details and ignore the contradiction.

**Questions to ask.** What can be definitely excluded? Which clues are mutually independent? What would I expect to see in the opposite direction if this location is right? Can a second analyst reach the same place without my notes?

sections.heading: Chronolocation: estimating when a photo was taken
sections.content:
**What it is.** Chronolocation estimates the time of day, date, or season from visual evidence. The most rigorous method uses the sun. A shadow is a clock whose face is the ground: its direction tells you where the sun is horizontally, and its length tells you how high the sun is.

**The geometry.** For an upright object of known height, the sun's elevation angle equals the arctangent of height divided by shadow length. A 2 m pole casting a 3.2 m shadow gives arctan(0.625), about 32 degrees of elevation. The shadow points directly away from the sun, so a shadow pointing west places the sun in the east, which is morning in most places. Estimate heights from references in the scene: door height around 2 m, standard road signs, rail gauge, parked car height.

**Using SunCalc.** SunCalc displays the sun's azimuth and elevation for a location and date on a map, plus sunrise and sunset lines. Once you have a candidate location, you can do two things. If the date is known or claimed, find the time when elevation matches your measurement and the direction matches the shadow. If the time is claimed, check whether the shadow geometry is consistent with that date. The claim is falsified when the angle cannot occur at that location on that date, for example a shadow that is much too short for a winter morning at high latitude.

**Other clues.**

- Weather: compare the scene (rain, fog, snow, cloud cover, wet pavement) against historical weather records from national meteorological services and open weather archives for the nearest station.
- Season: leaf cover, crops, snow, holiday decorations, clothing.
- Clocks and screens: station clocks, shop hours signs, phone status bars (time and battery), dashboard clocks, and posters for dated events. Sports fixtures and concerts have published dates.
- Construction state: a building site or a road project dated by news or imagery history gives a bracket.
- Reflections: moon phase, if visible, constrains the date.

**Pitfalls.** Shadow length on sloped ground is distorted, camera tilt and lens distortion skew angles, and building shadows are hard to measure without a base reference. Daylight saving time and time zones cause one-hour errors when converting clock readings. Several dates share the same sun elevation (two per year at the same time of day), so you need a second clue to choose.

**Questions to ask.** Is the chosen date the only one consistent with all clues? Which assumptions (object height, ground flatness) does my estimate rest on, and what is the error range?

sections.heading: Detecting manipulation, and the limits of the tools
sections.content:
**What it is.** Manipulation analysis asks whether an image was altered after capture: objects added or removed, text replaced, regions cloned, or the whole picture generated. Compare it to checking a signed document for erasures: you look for physical inconsistencies, not for a magic stamp.

**Visual tells (start here).** These are more reliable than automated filters. Look for inconsistent lighting direction between objects, shadows that do not agree with each other, edges with halos or unusually sharp or blurred borders, repeated texture patterns that indicate cloning, perspective that does not converge, reflections that do not match their source, and text with mismatched fonts, spacing, or anti-aliasing. For screenshots, compare UI elements with the real interface at the claimed version and date: icon styles, font rendering, button positions, language strings, scroll bars, and timestamp formats.

**Error level analysis (ELA).** ELA re-saves a JPEG at a known quality and shows the difference. Regions edited and saved at a different compression history may stand out. The caveats are large:

- High-contrast edges and detailed textures naturally appear bright, with no editing at all.
- Repeated re-compression by social platforms flattens the differences, so a forensic signal may vanish.
- Edits followed by a final uniform re-save can hide traces.
- Resized images and screenshots are poor candidates entirely.
- ELA output is a picture that invites over-interpretation; two people often read it differently.

Treat ELA as one prompt to look closer, never as a verdict. Other tools (noise residual views, JPEG quantization table comparison, double-compression detection, clone detection) have the same status.

**Structural checks.** Compare the embedded thumbnail with the main image, check whether the Software tag shows an editor, compare ModifyDate with DateTimeOriginal, and check whether the quantization tables match the claimed camera. Metadata can be forged, but forgers often make mistakes in less visible fields.

**Synthetic images.** AI-generated pictures often show inconsistent hands, text, jewelry, and background geometry, but those tells fade as models improve. Provenance signals such as content credentials (signed manifest data) can help when present; their absence proves nothing.

**Healthy skepticism.** Distinguish three outcomes: evidence of manipulation, evidence of authenticity, and inconclusive. Most real cases end as the third. Say so, and say what extra data (the original file, the sender's account history) would change the assessment.

sections.heading: Safe handling, ethics and legal limits
sections.content:
**Handle actor media as untrusted input.** Images can exploit parsers in viewers and editors, and links to 'proof' hosted by an actor can track your visit. Download in an isolated analysis environment, not your daily workstation. Hash the file on receipt (SHA-256) and keep the original read-only; do your work on copies. Do not browse the actor's infrastructure from your corporate network or logged-in accounts. Prefer archived or captured copies, and use a clean research identity that cannot be tied to the organization where operational security demands it, within your employer's policy.

**Do not engage or contaminate evidence.** Avoid commenting on, liking, or downloading through accounts that identify you. Record the source URL, retrieval time, tool versions, and every transformation applied. Chain of custody matters if the case goes to law enforcement, legal, or insurers.

**Privacy and proportionality.** Geolocation skills can identify a private home. The bar for use is a legitimate defensive purpose, tied to the incident, using the minimum necessary information.

- Do not geolocate or identify private individuals who are not part of the investigation, including family members in the background of a photo.
- Do not publish precise locations or identities of third parties; share findings through incident and legal channels.
- Facial recognition and biometric matching are regulated in many jurisdictions (for example under European data-protection law and some US state biometric statutes) and may require a lawful basis, assessment, or be barred altogether. Get legal advice before using them.
- Accessing a private account, bypassing authentication, or retrieving content not publicly available is not OSINT, and may be unlawful.
- Be careful with harmful imagery. If you encounter illegal content, stop, do not copy or distribute it, and escalate according to legal and policy instructions.

**Be honest about uncertainty.** Misidentification has real victims: wrongly attributing a photo to a person or place can harm them, and online communities have repeatedly misidentified suspects. Use graded language, state assumptions, and invite review.

**Questions to ask before you start.** Do I have authority and a defensive purpose? What is the minimum I need to learn? Who could be harmed if I am wrong? Where will the findings be stored, and who can see them?

sections.heading: Worked example: verifying a breach-proof screenshot and a photo
sections.content:
**The scenario.** An extortion post claims a breach of a fictional logistics company, Northwind Freight, and attaches two files: a PNG screenshot of an 'internal admin console' listing customer records, and a JPEG photo described as 'taken at the HQ data room last week'. Leadership wants to know how credible the claim is before deciding on a public statement.

**Step 1: preserve.** Download both files in an isolated environment, compute SHA-256 hashes, and record the source URL and retrieval time. Work on copies.

**Step 2: metadata.** Run exiftool -a -G1 -s on each file. The PNG has no camera tags, which is expected for a screenshot, and its pixel dimensions match a common laptop resolution. The JPEG carries Make and Model for a phone, DateTimeOriginal five months ago, an OffsetTimeOriginal of +02:00, and no GPS block. The ThumbnailImage tag shows the same scene, so no thumbnail mismatch. Absence of GPS means little: the phone's location setting may be off or removed.

**Step 3: screenshot content.** Compare the UI with the real console used by Northwind. The product name and layout match a vendor's public demo, and the toolbar icons belong to an older version than Northwind runs. Record fields are in a sample-data style (sequential IDs, placeholder-looking names). A crop of the table header searched in several reverse engines returns a vendor documentation page with the same layout, crawled two years earlier. Conclusion: the screenshot is consistent with a vendor demo, and inconsistent with the claimed system. This does not prove there was no breach.

**Step 4: photo geolocation.** The window shows a tram line with overhead wires, a bilingual street sign in two scripts, and a distinctive brick tower. Driving-side and sign languages narrow to a few countries; the tower, matched through map and street-level imagery, is in a city on a different continent from Northwind's HQ. The room contains no features unique to the HQ.

**Step 5: photo chronolocation.** A 1.8 m window frame casts a 2.9 m shadow across the floor, roughly 32 degrees elevation, pointing north-west, so in that hemisphere the sun is in the south-east, in the morning. SunCalc for the identified city places that elevation around mid-morning, in spring, consistent with the EXIF date and not with the claimed 'last week' date. Historical weather for that date shows clear skies, matching the picture.

**Step 6: write the assessment.**

| Item | Finding | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Screenshot | Matches a public vendor demo, not Northwind's system | High |
| Photo location | Not the HQ; different city | Medium-high |
| Photo date | About five months before the claim | Medium |
| Breach itself | Not determinable from these files | Requires internal telemetry |

**What to do next.** The images weaken the claim's credibility but cannot close the case. Pull authentication logs, data-access records, and egress telemetry, and check whether any supposed record exists in the real database. Report the image findings with assumptions and error ranges, and say clearly what you cannot determine.

quiz.question: You pull a photo of a supposed 'office walkthrough' from a social post and ExifTool shows no camera, date, or GPS tags. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.label: The file is almost certainly edited or fabricated, because genuine photos always keep their original metadata
The missing tags are uninformative on their own, since many services strip metadata on upload; seek the original file
The photo is authentic, because stripped metadata shows the owner took deliberate privacy precautions
The photo was certainly taken indoors, because outdoor photos always keep their GPS data intact

quiz.explanation: Platforms commonly re-encode uploads and remove EXIF, so a missing tag set is the normal state of a copy found on social media and tells you nothing about authenticity. The right move is to look for a closer-to-source copy, such as an original attachment, and to rely on content-based analysis meanwhile. Claiming fabrication from missing tags is wrong because stripping is routine. Claiming authenticity from missing tags is wrong because stripping can be done by anyone, including a forger. The indoor claim is invented, since outdoor photos lose GPS in the same way.

quiz.question: A 2 m pole in a photo casts a 3.2 m shadow. How do you use this to test a claimed time and place?

options.label: Divide the shadow length by the pole height to get the time of day directly, with no map data needed
Treat shadow length as irrelevant, because only the shadow direction can be compared with any sun data
Assume the sun was at 45 degrees, since shadows are considered reliable only at that elevation
Compute elevation as arctan(height / shadow), about 32 degrees, then compare with SunCalc for the claimed location and date

quiz.explanation: Shadow length gives the sun's elevation angle through the arctangent of height over length, here about 32 degrees, and direction gives the sun's azimuth. Comparing both with SunCalc output for the claimed place and date shows whether they can coexist. The ratio is not a time of day; elevation must be matched against a location-specific sun path. Length is highly relevant, not irrelevant. And no rule makes 45 degrees the only usable elevation; any elevation works if height and length are measured well.

quiz.question: An error level analysis image of a leaked photo shows bright areas along a building's sharp edges and a detailed tree. How should you treat this?

options.label: As a lead only, since high-contrast edges and fine texture appear bright in ELA without any edit; corroborate with other checks
As proof of splicing, because only edited regions can ever appear brighter than their surroundings
As proof of authenticity, because uniform brightness across the image would indicate manipulation
As meaningless, because ELA can only be run on screenshots and never on photographs saved in JPEG

quiz.explanation: ELA brightness is strongly affected by edges and texture, so bright regions can be perfectly natural. Used as a prompt to look closer and combined with lighting, shadow, thumbnail, and metadata checks, it has some value. Treating it as proof of splicing ignores the known false positives. Treating it as proof of authenticity ignores that re-saves can hide edits. And ELA is designed for JPEG photographs, which is where it is most applicable; screenshots and resized images are poor candidates.

quiz.question: You search a suspected fake recruiter's profile photo in three reverse-image engines and get no matches. What should you conclude?

options.label: The photo is original and the person is real, because a stolen image would have appeared in at least one engine
The photo must be AI-generated, because only generated faces fail to appear in image indexes
Nothing conclusive, since engines are not exhaustive; try crops, flips, other regions, and note it as inconclusive
The search method is broken, and you should only use face-recognition services that scan all private accounts

quiz.explanation: No engine indexes the whole web, and closed groups, private messages, and paywalled pages are invisible to all of them. No hits is therefore a gap in coverage, not a finding of originality. Trying crops, mirrored versions, and different engines can improve recall, and the result should be recorded as inconclusive. Declaring the person real or the image AI-generated overreaches from absence of evidence. Switching to services that scan private accounts would be unlawful and ethically unacceptable.

quiz.question: Your CISO asks you to check whether your own public website and press photos leak sensitive details. Which approach is best?

options.label: Ask employees to confirm that they never enabled location on their phones, and treat that as the audit
Check only the main logo files, since decorative photos cannot contain anything that matters to attackers
Download the public originals as an outsider would, run exiftool recursively for GPS, serial, author, and edit history, and also review visible content
Rely on the CDN's compression to remove everything, then confirm by viewing a few images in a browser

quiz.explanation: An audit should reproduce what an attacker can do: fetch the images as published, run bulk metadata extraction, and list files carrying coordinates, device serials, author names, or editor history, then also review content such as screens, badges, and window views that survive stripping. Self-reporting by staff is unreliable and untestable. Looking only at logos misses the photos where leakage actually occurs. Assuming a CDN strips metadata is an unverified claim, and viewing in a browser never shows EXIF anyway.
